newsitem.title: DUBAI: Albright's priorities may disappoint Gulf Arabs.
newsitem.headline: Albright's priorities may disappoint Gulf Arabs.

text.p: New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright appears to have put the Middle East and the Gulf on the back-burner as she settles in to the Clinton administration's top foreign policy post, Gulf-based analysts said on Sunday.
Albright's much-travelled predecessor Warren Christopher visited the troubled area more often than any other.
But Albright, speaking to reporters shortly after taking over at the State Department on Friday, said her first foreign foray would be to Europe and Asia next month.
On the Middle East, she said she would be guided by the advice of special coordinator Dennis Ross.
Gulf Arab oil-producers who rely on the United States for protection against much larger regional powers may be concerned by the region's apparent relegation.

"The Gulf Arabs look to Washington to come to their aid in times of tension and to be seen to be doing so in a very high-profile manner," one analyst said. "The Americans haven't let their allies down, as we saw in the Gulf War.
"But if the Clinton administration is now signalling a lower priority for the Gulf on its list of foreign policy issues, there will be some nervousness around here."

Albright's appointment received wide coverage in the region but Gulf Arab governments maintained their usual cautious approach to publicly commenting on international politics and one official said on Sunday that was unlikely to change.

But Gulf News daily, which often reflects popular sentiment, called on Albright to reverse Clinton's "disaster-prone foreign policy" and adopt a shrewder stance towards Iran and Iraq in place of the "misguided" policy of dual containment.
While Gulf Arab states remain fearful of Iran and Iraq, some question the scale of U.S. intervention in the region, where the monarchies would be most vulnerable in a full-scale conflict.
Gulf News said Washington's restrictions on U.S. firms investing in Iranian projects had proved counter-productive, apart from angering Europe.
Albright would be clearing a skeleton in the State Department cupboard if she succeeded in persuading Clinton to end the policy.

Ominously, the Middle East was not high on her priority list, Gulf News said. She had no plans to go to the region in the immediate future, which suggested she was satisfied with the pro-Israeli stance that Clinton had maintained from the start.
Albright said at Friday's news conference achieving a comprehensive peace was a very high priority for Clinton and therefore also for her.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters in Cairo on Saturday before leaving for a brief visit to Saudi Arabia that he and Albright discussed the Middle East peace process and "she assured me that it was one of Washington's priorities".

Albright described Iran and Iraq as rogue states which "not only do not see an advantage to a functioning international system, but...feel that they are more important when they can disrupt the international system."
Henry Kissinger, one of Albright's most influential predecessors, contends that the Gulf cannot be overlooked.
Writing in Newsweek, he said that while the Arab-Israeli issue was demonstrably explosive, even more dangerous structural issues lurked below the surface of the Gulf.
"There, states of very limited power possess the capacity to cause nearly infinite international damage," Kissinger said.

When the Gulf states raised oil prices by 387 percent in a three-month period in 1973, they triggered a 10-year financial and economic crisis that threatened the global economic and financial systems and undermined the governability of the industrial democracies, he said.

Today, the consequences of a Gulf crisis were no less ominous but the structure on which its stability depended was even more brittle. The two strongest nations, Iran and Iraq, were outlaw states and the immediate area contained only two friendly Islamic countries, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

"But Saudi Arabia is going through the torments of adapting an essentially feudal society to the modernisation wrought by oil resources, global communications and the spread of education. Jordan, bordering Iraq, Syria and Israel, has its hands full with its own immediate security concerns...
"To seek stability in the Gulf against both Iran and Iraq simultaneously, with vulnerable Saudi Arabia our only ally, is a high-risk policy," Kissinger added.
